job: Hydraulic steering rack (rack and pinion) replacement
unit: per job: one hydraulic power steering rack / steering gear assembly (rack and pinion), fitted, with the power steering fluid refilled and the system bled. All four examples are older vehicles with hydraulic power steering (a belt-driven pump and fluid); electric racks are covered in a separate estimate. Low = a remanufactured or new aftermarket rack whose page states which it is, high = the genuine part at list (MSRP). Any refundable core charge on a remanufactured rack is left out of the price. Not included: the wheel alignment afterwards (see extras), outer tie rod ends, hoses, the pump, a full system flush, and diagnosis

benchmarks.name: RepairPal (Honda Accord page)
benchmarks.note: by model year, hydraulic-steering years only: 2003-2007 Accord $1,953-$2,136; 2008, 2009 and 2010 Accord $3,539-$3,813; 2011-2012 $2,291-$2,565 (2000-2002 $1,210-$1,450). The page shows no parts and labor split for these years. Its all-years figure, $2,824-$3,105, mixes in later electric-rack cars

benchmarks.name: RepairPal (Honda Civic page)
benchmarks.note: 2012-2015 Civic $2,354-$2,536, the oldest years the page labels; the 2006-2011 years are not labelled on the page as loaded. Same publisher as the entry above, so not an independent second opinion

benchmarks.name: PartsAvatar (parts retailer article)
benchmarks.note: a Canadian parts retailer's unsigned article (footer 2023): the rack 'can vary from $500 to $2000' plus 'labor costs varying between $150 - $300', which add to $650-$2,300, and $100-$150 more for an alignment. Currency is not stated and is probably Canadian dollars. It also says the job 'takes 4 to 6 hours' on average and '2 to 8 hours' depending on the vehicle; a general article, not used for the hours

finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so there is nothing to call too wide or too narrow; this file is a first build and the hydraulic counterpart to the electric-rack estimate. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2008 Honda Civic about $452-$2,622; midsize 2010 Honda Accord 2.4L about $554-$2,345; truck 2009 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 about $723-$1,573; luxury 2008 Acura TL about $623-$2,289. So about $450-$2,650 covers the four examples. The spread is almost entirely the part: a remanufactured or new aftermarket hydraulic rack was seen at $212-$483, while the genuine Honda and Acura racks list at $1,649-$1,982 and GM's own (remanufactured) kit at $902-$933. A shop that fits an aftermarket rack and marks it up will usually land between the two ends, and adds an alignment. How solid the labor times are: weak. All four classes rest on one source, a rack-replacement instruction sheet on the remanufacturer Cardone's site that says 2-4 hours 'depending on application'. It is a parts-maker time, not a time for any of the example vehicles, and no maker-stated or book time for replacing a hydraulic rack on the Civic, Accord, Silverado or TL was found: the Honda and Acura documents for these cars cover hoses, pumps and columns, and GM's bulletins point to its labor guide without printing the time. Two cross-checks support the range: Toyota and Lexus allow 2.8 and 2.9 (no unit printed) to remove, reseal and refit a hydraulic rack on the 2004-2010 Sienna and 2004-2009 RX, and Honda's stated times for the later electric Accord rack are 3.2-3.8 hours including alignment. Parts cautions: the Civic and Accord lows are MAVAL remanufactured racks from one retailer; the Silverado and TL lows are new Cardone racks from one retailer; the TL page adds a $13.20 core deposit that is left out, and no other page showed a core charge, though remanufactured racks often carry one at the counter. A cheaper TL rack (MAVAL, $207.34) was not used because its page does not say new or remanufactured. The Silverado high is GM's remanufactured kit at list because the one new genuine gear listed has no price; the Silverado example is a 2009 truck because that is the year the GM catalog page loaded for, and the aftermarket rack fits 2007-2013. A Japan-built 2010 Accord 2.4L takes a different genuine rack listing at $3,117, far above the high used here. Benchmarks: RepairPal's Accord page gives $1,953-$2,136 for 2003-2007 cars and $3,539-$3,813 for 2008-2010 cars, well above the built totals; the likely reason is that it prices the genuine rack plus more labor, but the page shows no parts and labor split, so that is a reading, not a finding. Only two independent publishers could be loaded as benchmarks (two of the three entries are RepairPal pages), short of the three asked for. Confidence is low because no labor time is for an example vehicle and each low rests on a single retailer. This is an estimate, not a quote and not a diagnosis.
extras: A quote nearly always adds a wheel alignment, which is not included here. Also common: outer tie rod ends, a full power steering fluid flush and an in-line filter (rack remanufacturers often require both for their warranty), pressure or return hoses, the pump if it failed or sent debris into the old rack, new mounting bolts or bushings, a refundable core charge on a remanufactured rack, a diagnosis fee, shop supplies and sales tax. If the subframe has to be lowered to get the rack out, labor rises. Before paying for a rack, have the leak traced: a leak at a hose connection or seal can look like a rack leak and costs far less to fix, and some hose leaks on these cars were recall repairs done by the dealer at no charge.
